what: Cava Group runs a fast-casual restaurant chain serving Mediterranean food. Customers build a bowl or pita from a line of grains, proteins, dips and toppings. It owns and operates nearly all its restaurants rather than franchising, and also sells dips and spreads in supermarkets.
customers: Mostly younger urban and suburban customers in the United States, eating in, taking away or ordering through delivery apps.
money: Food and drink sold in its own restaurants and through digital ordering.
Dips and spreads sold through grocery retailers.
moat: Cava occupies a category with almost no national competitor: Mediterranean food at a fast-casual price, built on the assembly-line format that Chipotle proved works. Owning rather than franchising means it controls the experience and keeps all the economics, and its individual restaurants generate unusually high sales per location, which is the single best predictor of whether a restaurant chain can expand profitably.
risks: The shares trade at about 95 times earnings, 39 times EV/EBITDA and 150 times free cash flow. The price assumes many years of rapid, profitable expansion with nothing going wrong.
Restaurant expansion is where growth stories break: the best locations are taken first, and later openings usually earn less than earlier ones.
Net income of $64.7M and free cash flow of $40.0M are small in absolute terms, so the valuation rests on what the restaurants might earn rather than what they do earn.
Fast-casual is intensely competitive and fashion-sensitive, and the customer is young and willing to move on.
Twenty-four analysts average a $75.42 target against a $51.23 price, a 47% gap that signals wide disagreement about the growth rate.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $500.1M in 2021 to $1.2B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $1.4B.
Sales per restaurant are high by fast-casual standards, which is the strongest evidence that new openings can earn their cost of capital.
The restaurant count is still small relative to the United States, so the runway for new openings is genuinely long if the economics hold.
Mediterranean food fits the direction of consumer preference toward food seen as fresh and healthy, which is a durable rather than faddish trend.
Cash of $282.9M against $466.2M of debt funds expansion without immediate financing pressure.
watch: Sales per restaurant at locations open more than a year, and the return on the cost of building a new one. Those two decide whether opening more restaurants creates value or merely creates more restaurants.
view: Restaurant growth stories follow a script and it is worth knowing the script before reading any of the numbers. A chain opens in its best markets first, where the restaurants do extraordinary volumes and the returns on each build look wonderful. Investors extrapolate those returns across hundreds of future locations and assign a very large multiple. Then the chain runs out of great sites, opens in ordinary ones, the average sales per restaurant falls, and the multiple collapses — not because anything went wrong, but because the early returns were never the average.

Cava is somewhere in the early part of that script, and the important thing is that it is doing the early part unusually well. Sales per restaurant are high by fast-casual standards, which is the single most reliable indicator of whether a concept can expand profitably — it tells you customers genuinely want this rather than merely tolerating it. The category is also close to empty: there is no national Mediterranean fast-casual chain, and the assembly-line format has been proven to work by Chipotle. That combination is rare and it is why the market is paying what it is.

What the market is paying is 95 times earnings, 39 times EV/EBITDA and 150 times free cash flow for a company earning $65 million. At that price you are not buying today’s restaurants; you are buying several hundred that do not exist yet, and assuming they will perform like the current ones. The twenty-four analysts averaging $75 against a $51 share price are arguing about exactly this, and the spread between them tells you nobody is confident.

So the question is narrow and it is answerable from the disclosures: what do restaurants open more than a year do in sales, is that figure holding as the estate grows, and what return does a new build earn on its cost? If sales per restaurant hold while the count doubles, this justifies a high multiple and the only argument is how high. If they drift down as openings move into secondary markets, the script runs its usual course. I would be watching that number rather than quarterly earnings, which at this stage tell you almost nothing.
bull: Sales per restaurant hold as the estate expands, new builds keep earning high returns on cost, and Cava fills an empty national category the way Chipotle filled its own.
bear: The best sites are already taken, later openings earn ordinary returns, average sales per restaurant drift down, and a 95 times earnings multiple reprices to a normal restaurant chain.
